facts.statement: The genus Squatinactis was discovered in 1974 by Richard Lund.
facts.quote: This fish was discovered in 1974 by Richard Lund.

facts.statement: Squatinactis is an extinct cartilaginous fish known from the Carboniferous-aged Bear Gulch Limestone in Montana.
facts.quote: Squatinactis is a genus of extinct elasmobranch chondrichthyan known from the Carboniferous aged Bear Gulch Limestone in Montana.

facts.statement: Squatinactis had broad pectoral fins that resembled those of modern stingrays and angel sharks.
facts.quote: This creature's most startling feature were its broad pectoral fins which resembled those of stingrays and angel sharks (Squatina).

facts.statement: The holotype specimen of Squatinactis possessed approximately 15 teeth in its jaw.
facts.quote: The holotype specimen has about 15 teeth in its jaw.

facts.statement: Squatinactis had a flattened body equipped with a set of large pectoral fins.
facts.quote: Squatinactis had a flattened body with a set of large pectoral fins.

facts.statement: The pectoral fins of Squatinactis were pointed forward and measured around two feet in length.
facts.quote: The fins were oddly pointed forward, with a length of around two feet long.

facts.statement: Squatinactis had a short snout and a wide mouth containing long, conical, cladodont-shaped teeth.
facts.quote: The snout was short and the wide mouth was equipped with a series of long conical cladodont-shaped teeth.

facts.statement: The body of Squatinactis was covered in only a few placoid scales, leaving most of the surface bare.
facts.quote: The body was covered in a few placoid scales, but most of the surface was bare.

facts.statement: Squatinactis is classified within the Elasmobranchii, specifically in its own order, Squatinactiformes.
facts.quote: This fish is currently classified within the Elasmobranchii, more specially in its own grouping, the Squatinactiformes.

facts.statement: Squatinactis was likely a benthic predator that lived half-buried in the sand and lunged at nearby prey.
facts.quote: This fish was probably a benthic predator; it probably lived half-buried in the sand and suddenly emerged to throw itself against the prey swimming nearby.

facts.statement: The wing-like fins and long tail of Squatinactis were likely used for propulsion while moving along the seabed.
facts.quote: The wing-like fins and long tail were most likely useful for propulsion from the seabed.

facts.statement: Squatinactis lived during the Serpukhovian stage, between 326.9 and 323.6 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Serpukhovian to Serpukhovian (326.9 to 323.6 million years ago)

rejected.statement: Squatinactis had a long, whip-like tail featuring a spine that was actually a modified secondary dorsal fin.
rejected.quote: It also had a long, whip-like tail with a spine (a feature analogous to some rays) that was actually a modified, secondary dorsal fin.
